why: The business is not broken. It is a near-duopoly in a service people cannot skip, it converts profit to cash, and at {fwd.0.pe|x1} forward earnings you are not paying for growth you have to believe in.
But the earnings engine is financial, not operational. Revenue grew 5%; EPS grew 56%. The difference is a 23% smaller share count bought with borrowed money at 3.37x leverage and a 5.43% coupon.

And this stock has told you exactly what it cares about. Over eight quarters it has risen on one thing only — a higher guidance midpoint. It got two of those, worth +21% and +23%. Every other quarter it fell.

The genuine bull case is expanded HD: better middle-molecule clearance may cut mortality, and a larger surviving census is the volume growth this company does not have. That is quarters away, not priced, and worth watching.
I want a lower price or one clean quarter of commercial mix stabilising before this is a position, not a watch.

notes.title: Open on the number, not the company. DaVita went up 145% in seven months and gave back a quarter of it in three days — and it did that on its strongest quarter in six, with revenue, margin and EPS all up. That contradiction is the whole video. Tell them we're going to find out exactly why, using the filings, not the headlines.
notes.tape: Walk the tape left to right. January low of 101. Then two guidance increases took it to 247 by August 3rd. Earnings came out after the close on the 4th. On the 5th it opened at 205 and closed at 188 — down 17 percent in one day on nearly four million shares, five times normal volume. Point out that the market did not misread this. Something in the release genuinely changed the story.
notes.business: Keep this short and physical. DaVita runs dialysis clinics. If your kidneys fail you go three times a week, for the rest of your life or until a transplant. 3,266 clinics, 298,500 patients, 92,649 treatments every single day. Say the important part out loud: this is the most recurring revenue in healthcare. Nobody skips dialysis in a recession. That's why the market is willing to lever it up. TARGET 25s.
notes.payor: This is the slide that explains everything else — slow down here. 11 percent of DaVita's patients have commercial insurance. Those 11 percent generate 26 percent of the revenue. And read DaVita's own sentence off the screen: 'the payments we receive from commercial payors generate nearly all of our profits.' Their words, in the 10-K. So when you analyse DaVita you are not really analysing 298,500 patients. You are analysing about 33,000 of them. Everything else roughly washes. TARGET 30s.
notes.twoprices: Now make it concrete with the arithmetic. Blended, they collect $415.87 per treatment and spend $277.40 delivering it. But that blend hides two completely different businesses. Back out the 11/26 split and a government treatment brings in roughly $346 against a $277 cost — call it seventy dollars. A commercial treatment brings in roughly $980 — about seven hundred dollars of margin. Flag clearly that this is MY derivation from their disclosure, not a number they print. Then the punchline: a 1 percent shift from commercial to government does more damage than a 1 percent move in anything else on the income statement. TARGET 30s.
notes.commercial: So here is what actually happened this quarter. Government revenue grew 5.4 percent. Commercial revenue — the profitable 11 percent — went DOWN 0.7 percent. In dollars, government added 105 million and commercial lost 7 million. Commercial's share of the mix dropped from 32.6 to 31.3 percent. That's 128 basis points off the only line that carries profit. This is the single most important number in the release and it is buried in a footnote on page 7. TARGET 30s.
notes.rpt: The mix shift shows up immediately in the headline metric. Revenue per treatment went DOWN sequentially, 417.59 to 415.87. And read the company's own explanation: the decline was 'driven by changes in payor mix.' For a company whose volume grows 0.3 percent, price per treatment IS the growth. It just went backwards. TARGET 20s.
notes.volume: And there is no volume to fall back on. Normalized non-acquired treatment growth — that's their own metric, stripping out acquisitions and calendar effects — was 0.3 percent. Not 3. Zero point three. This company does not grow by treating more people. It grows by price, by buying clinics, and by buying its own stock. Remember that for the verdict. TARGET 20s.
notes.headline: Now the part everyone else's video stops at. On the surface this was a strong quarter. Revenue 3.55 billion. Operating income 579 million, a 16.3 percent margin, the best since December 2024. EPS 4.02 against 2.87 last quarter. If you only read the press release headline you'd expect this stock UP. So why was it down 17?
notes.bridge: Here's why. Operating income went up 97 million quarter over quarter. Break it into three pieces. The core US dialysis business — 85 percent of revenue — contributed 32 million. Corporate costs swung 14 million. And the ancillary segment went from 6 million to 57 million — a 51 million dollar swing. That one small segment is 53 percent of the entire increase. The business everybody thinks they're buying produced a third of it.
notes.quality: And that 51 million is the softest kind of profit there is. Ancillary is mostly integrated kidney care — value-based contracts where you get paid later, after the health plan settles up. Two numbers from the 10-Q. One: in the first half they booked 98.5 million of revenue for work performed in PREVIOUS years. Two: contract assets — revenue earned but not yet billed — went from 310 million to 399 million in six months. So the segment that carried the quarter is recognising old work and building unbilled receivables. That is not the same thing as cash.
notes.guidance: And management told you so, without saying it. Their best quarter in six, and they left full-year guidance completely untouched — 14.10 to 15.20, character for character the same as May 5th. Now do the arithmetic they hoped you wouldn't. First half was 6.86. That leaves 7.24 to 8.34 for the second half. Q2 alone annualises to 8.04 — at the TOP of that range. And that's with the share count still shrinking, which mechanically adds EPS. Strip that out and the midpoint says second-half earnings power goes DOWN from here.
notes.cash: Cash says the same thing. Trailing twelve month free cash flow is 1.31 billion and that looks great. But first-half free cash flow was only 396 million — 140 in Q1, 256 in Q2. Full-year guidance is 1.0 to 1.25 billion. So the second half has to produce roughly 600 to 850 million, more than double the first half. Every dollar of that is already spoken for by buybacks and interest. TARGET 25s.
notes.engine: So where did 56 percent EPS growth come from on 5 percent revenue growth? Here. Share count went from 85.8 million to 64.0 million — they have retired roughly a quarter of the company in two years. 751 million of buybacks in the first half alone. That is the entire earnings story. And it is funded with debt: 10.2 billion net, leverage climbing 3.27 to 3.37 times, at 5.43 percent, and they added another 500 million term loan in June. Shareholders' equity is NEGATIVE 765 million — say clearly this is a buyback artefact, not insolvency, but it does mean there is no cushion. TARGET 35s.
notes.buyprice: One more thing nobody will show you. Look at what they've been PAYING. 122 dollars in January. 134 in Q1. 155 in Q2. And then between July 1st and August 4th they paid 199.55 — that was settling the Berkshire obligation on July 31st. Three trading days later the stock was 181. I am not saying management should time the market. I am saying a buyback is only value creation if you buy below intrinsic value, and this one has been chasing the price up. TARGET 25s.
notes.medicare: Now the 2027 problem, and this is in the 10-Q from June. Medicare is 57 percent of dialysis revenue. CMS gave them a 2.2 percent raise for 2026. The proposed rule for 2027 is 1.1 percent — half. Meanwhile their own cost per treatment is running 3.2 percent higher year over year. That is negative jaws on 57 percent of the business, starting in eighteen months. Nothing about that is priced into a 12 times multiple being 'cheap.' TARGET 25s.
notes.valuation: Alright, so what's it worth. At 181.50 you're paying 12.3 times this year's expected earnings and 9.8 times next year's. Trailing free cash flow yield is over 11 percent. That is objectively cheap. But — and this is the bit beginners miss — market cap is only 11.6 billion. Add 10.2 billion of net debt and you are actually buying a 21.8 billion dollar enterprise. On that basis it's about 9.9 times operating profit. Cheap-ish. Not a giveaway. The Street has a 240 target and still rates it a Hold, which tells you they agree the number is cheap and don't trust it either. TARGET 30s.
notes.verdict: Bring it home. Six things, scored. Margins and valuation are genuinely strong. Balance sheet is the risk. Revenue quality is weak because the only profitable payor went backwards. Cash and capital allocation are mixed. Then my call: WATCH, not buy. Say why in one line — the business is fine, the price is fine, the financing is what makes it fragile. Then walk the calculator: 4 percent growth, 15.5 percent margins, 11 times exit, 6 percent annual share shrink, and show what falls out. Remind them these are MY assumptions and they should change them and see what happens. TARGET 40s.
notes.handoff: That's the business. Fundamentals tell you what to own — they never tell you when. Let's go to the chart. TARGET 8s.
notes.history: This is the slide that proves it, and nobody else will have made this. I pulled the guidance table out of the last eight earnings releases and lined it up against what the stock did the very next session. Look at the pattern. Five times management revised the year inside the year. Four times they left the midpoint alone or just narrowed the range — the stock fell every single one, down as much as seventeen. One time they raised it, this May — plus twenty-three percent in a day. The grey bars are the January guides for a brand new year, which aren't a fair comparison so I'm excluding them. The takeaway: this stock does not trade on earnings, it trades on the guidance midpoint. On August 4th the midpoint didn't move. If you knew this pattern, the 17 percent drop was not a surprise at all.
notes.indexed: Here is the question that decides whether 12 times earnings is actually cheap. Both lines start at 100 a year ago. The blue steps up each time they reported — that's trailing earnings, and it only moves on the day the market found out. The orange is the share price. Earnings went up 17 percent over the year. The price went up 41 percent even after the crash. So the stock did not rise because the business got better by that much — it rose because the market agreed to pay a higher multiple. That is exactly the kind of gain that comes back out when guidance disappoints, and last week it did.
notes.street: Quick one. The average analyst target is 240 against 181 today — a 33 percent gap. And the same panel rates it a Hold. Two strong buys, three holds, one sell. That combination is unusual and it tells you something: everyone can see the number is low, nobody wants to be the person holding the leverage when Medicare resets. Note it's only six analysts covering this — thin coverage.
notes.twolists: Let me put both sides up honestly, because I don't want you buying or avoiding this on my word. Left side, what's genuinely working: a service nobody can skip, best margin since 2024, two billion of operating cash flow, a quarter of the company retired, twelve times earnings. Right side, what worries me: no volume growth, the profitable payor shrinking, ten billion of net debt with negative equity, Medicare's raise getting halved, and half of last quarter's profit jump coming from a lumpy segment. Every one of those ten lines traces to a filing. Read both columns and see which side you land on.
notes.findings: Before the numbers, here is what you are getting here that you will not get from a headline recap. Four things, all of them out of DaVita's filings. One: the only payor that carries profit went backwards. Two: half the quarter's profit jump came from a segment booking old work. Three: eight quarters of guidance tables explain the whole stock in one pattern. Four: they bought their own shares at 199 dollars three days before the stock was 181. Read them, promise to walk each, move on.
